results.thread: 1. Who you are and what your job is
results.text: If I say nothing for a month, what happens to my real money and to the paper books?
results.answer: Sir, your real money does nothing: it stays exactly as it is in your Zerodha account, because nothing is ever placed from chat and I can't trade it. The paper books keep running on their own: each evening I re-rate your holdings and write the cut list, the managed copy of your account acts on it on paper, and the practice book and options line keep recording trades. The guardrails keep running too (a 5% loss stops the paper day), and the drafts waiting for your yes simply stay waiting. results.text: If RSI is 28 on the Nifty daily, what does that tell you, and what would you do?
results.answer: Sir, an RSI (a 0-100 gauge) of 28 would mean oversold: the Nifty has fallen hard and fast, but that alone is not a buy signal. results.text: On a sideways day with low volume, do you trade or stay out?
results.answer: Sir, I'd mostly stay out. On a quiet, sideways day there is little movement to pay for the costs. Ananta's intraday test found that a wide first 15 minutes came before a wider rest of the day (1.64% against 0.96%), so a narrow, low-volume open points to a small day. Its breakout tests also barely made money after costs even on normal days, and buying options on a flat day only gives time decay. If you do trade, keep it small and wait for the price to leave the day's range on rising volume rather than guessing the direction.
results.wanted: A direct answer on whether to trade or stay out on a sideways, low-volume day, with a specific reason rather than generic advice.
results.missing: It leans on a general claim ('barely made money after costs') without quantifying it, and the conditional 'if you do trade' advice, wait for a range exit on rising volume, was not tested by Ananta, nor does it say how this applies to the paper book.

results.text: If the Nifty closes 20% above its 50-day average, what has your testing found?
results.answer: Sir, Ananta hasn't tested that on the Nifty itself; the test was on individual stocks. On the 250 most traded stocks, buying more than 20% above the 50-day average earned about 2.5% less over the next 20 sessions than other buys (-2.5% in 2000-2017, -2.4% in 2018-2023). A related teacher test found that uptrend stocks bought 8-15% above it earned about 1-1.5% less over 20 sessions, but that gap faded by 60 sessions. So the finding is "don't chase a stretched move", a filter on what to avoid and not a sell signal, and it shouldn't be carried over to the index without its own test.

results.text: What is the one risk rule that stops a bad day from becoming a bad month?
results.answer: Sir, the one rule is the daily loss stop: when realised plus open loss reaches 5% of the account's value at the start of the session, every position is closed and no new entry is made that day. That caps one bad day at about 5%, so it cannot snowball. The second line of defence is the rule that pauses trading after a 22% fall: when equity falls 22% below its high-water mark, new entries stop until you resume. Overnight gaps can exceed the 5% limit, because it acts during market hours only.
results.wanted: The single risk rule that keeps one bad day from turning into a bad month, named with its specific trigger and number.
results.missing: It names a daily loss stop and a 22% drawdown pause, but never says whether these rules apply to the new managed paper book (which has a 7% fixed stop and a 20-session minimum hold), and it doesn't make clear that it is all paper; the second rule also blurs the 'one rule' ask, and its 5% and 22% figures can't be checked against the conversation, so the answer looks well-formed but unverified.
